subject: Culture
title: Gift Economies and Debt
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Gift Economies and Debt.

hook.text: In Papua New Guinea a chief who gives away more than he keeps gains the most power.

buildup.text: Marcel Mauss described gift economies where giving creates an obligation. Receiving without returning is shameful.

discovery.text: The potlatch ceremonies of Pacific Northwest tribes were competitive feasts of destruction and generosity.

twist.text: Colonial governments banned potlatch in 1884 because gift-based power threatened capitalist market logic.

climax.text: Modern tipping culture is a shadow of gift economics—refusing to tip marks you as socially flawed.

punchline.text: Generosity is the oldest power move.

quiz.question: Who wrote the foundational study of gift economies?

details.summary: Gift economies create honor through generosity and debt. Marcel Mauss argued that gifts are never free — they create obligations to reciprocate. In potlatch cultures, giving away the most wealth conferred the highest status.
details.whyItMatters: Gift economies challenge capitalist assumptions that exchange requires markets. They reveal how generosity creates power and how debt creates social bonds that money cannot replicate.
takeaways: Marcel Mauss's 'The Gift' revealed obligation hidden in exchange
Potlatch cultures gained status by giving away wealth, not accumulating it
Gift debts create social bonds stronger than legal contracts

faq.question: How do gift economies create power?
faq.answer: In gift economies, the giver gains social power over the receiver — the recipient is indebted until they reciprocate. Giving lavishly demonstrates surplus wealth and creates dependent relationships. In potlatch cultures, the most generous chief held the most power.

faq.question: What did Marcel Mauss discover about gifts?
faq.answer: Mauss's 1925 essay 'The Gift' revealed three universal obligations in gift exchange: the obligation to give, the obligation to receive, and the obligation to reciprocate. Refusing a gift insults the giver. Accepting creates a debt.
